problem: Real-world robots need to find a goal specified by an image in a new outdoor environment. Prior approaches do not handle this well. Geometric and frontier mapping needs reliable depth and ignores semantic traversability (tall grass versus a fence). RL novelty or curiosity exploration needs more than 1M samples and only judges novelty after a state is visited. Earlier learned topological-graph navigators (SPTM, ViNG) have no explicit mechanism for exploring unseen environments or transferring prior experience to them.
motivation: Collecting new experience at deployment time is costly. Large offline datasets from other environments contain reusable navigational affordances. A robot therefore needs three things: generalization from offline data, robustness to non-stationary distractors (lighting, season, new obstacles), and a way to propose useful places to explore. The key observation is that a goal representation conditioned on the current observation and compressed by an information bottleneck gives all three: a compact, distractor-invariant goal code; a feasibility and uncertainty signal; and a prior from which reachable subgoals can be sampled.
key_idea: Learn a context-conditioned variational-information-bottleneck latent goal model that predicts actions and temporal distances from offline real-robot data. Sample latent subgoals from its prior to explore frontier nodes of an incrementally built non-parametric image topological graph, then plan over that graph to reach goals again.
insight: The encoder and decoder are conditioned on the current observation, so the latent encodes only the goal's relative position. Samples from the N(0,I) prior therefore decode into feasible nearby goals, unlike a plain VAE over images, and the prior density doubles as a goal-feasibility test. The ablations (Table 2, subset of unseen environments) support this: (1) removing the bottleneck (Vanilla Sampling) raises exploration time from 09:56 to 14:06 and lowers SCT from 0.92 to 0.83, and it fails on distant goals. (2) Replacing goal sampling with random action sequences at the frontier (the ECR variant) gives 14:54 and SCT 0.73. (3) Removing the topological graph (Reactive) hurts exploration only mildly (11:54) but badly hurts re-navigation (00:37.4, SCT 0.63), so goal sampling drives exploration while the memory drives recall. In undirected exploration, rollouts to sampled goals cover the environment about 5x faster than random actions (Fig. 6).
method: Context-conditioned latent goal model (VIB): encoder p_phi(z|o_t,o_g) maps the stacked current and goal RGB images (6x160x120) through MobileNet to a 1024-d feature, then to a 64-d Gaussian latent. Decoder q_theta(a,d|z,o_t) takes a separate MobileNet feature of o_t concatenated with z (1088-d) and predicts a 2-d action (continuous linear/angular velocity) and a 1-d temporal distance. Training maximizes the log-likelihood of actions and distances minus beta*KL(p_phi||N(0,I)), with beta=1.0, batch 128, Adam lr 1e-4.

Self-supervised offline data: time-correlated random-walk trajectories on a Clearpath Jackal. LiDAR/IMU collision detection splits walks into collision-free segments, and time steps serve as distance labels via hindsight relabeling (BADGR-style).
Feasibility test via the prior: if r(z_t^g) > epsilon (1e-2), the goal is judged in-distribution and reachable, and the robot heads straight to the goal latent.

Frontier exploration with a topological memory: nodes are egocentric images with visitation counts, and edges are predicted distances. LeastExploredNeighbor picks the lowest-count node within delta2=15. If the robot is at that frontier node (distance < delta1=4), it samples a latent subgoal from the prior r(z); otherwise it navigates to the frontier node.

SubgoalNavigate / ExpandGraph / online fine-tuning: roll out the decoder policy toward a fixed latent for H=5 s, update counts at the endpoint, add the new node and its edges, and fine-tune the model on the newly collected data for gamma=10 epochs.
Goal reaching after exploration (Alg. 2): associate the current and goal images to graph vertices, run a shortest path over predicted-distance edges, and follow node images as successive subgoals.

setting.backbone: Two MobileNet encoders + FC layers forming a conditional VIB latent goal/action/distance model (trained on offline robot data, fine-tuned online in each new environment)
setting.training_data: Offline real-world self-supervised random-walk data from training environments: 20 hours used for training all methods (Sec. 5.1). The released dataset has over 5000 trajectories / over 40 hours across 9 outdoor environments, collected over 18 months and partly reused from BADGR and ViNG. Online fine-tuning on data collected during exploration of each test environment.
setting.observation: monocular forward-facing 170° FOV RGB camera (160x120) + RGB goal image; no depth, GPS or odometry at test time
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity; subgoal rollouts of H=5 s
setting.privileged: none (GPS and LiDAR used only as safety controllers during data collection; re-navigation uses the map the robot built itself during exploration)

numbers_note: Real-world only, with no standard benchmark. Table 1 aggregates 8 unseen environments with one goal each. Per-environment exploration and navigation times appear only in Figure 8 (bar chart). Times are given as mm:ss strings exactly as printed. SCT is printed on a 0-1 scale and converted to 0-100 here. NTS was excluded because it failed in every environment. The Table 2 ablation environment subset is not specified. The 5x faster undirected-exploration result is shown only qualitatively in Fig. 6, and the non-stationarity robustness results only as trajectories in Fig. 5.
results: Across 8 unseen outdoor environments on a Clearpath Jackal, RECON discovers image-specified goals up to 80 m away in 09:54 on average. The best other methods are the ECR-style variant (14:54), ViNG (19:48), ANS (21:00), PPO+RND (21:18) and InfoBot (23:36). On the second traversal RECON reaches the goal in 00:26 with SCT 0.92, against 0.73 for ECR and 0.60 for ViNG. RL-based baselines only find goals within about 25 m, and NTS fails everywhere. The learned map and policy also stay valid under unseen obstacles (trash cans, cones, a car) and lighting changes (sunny, overcast, twilight).
limitations: Does not explicitly account for the value of information during exploration, and offers no theoretical guarantees on when the bottleneck or stochastic policy yields efficient exploration (stated by the authors).
Evaluation is small-scale real-world only: 8 environments with one goal image each, no success rates over many episodes, and times averaged without variance. Robustness results are qualitative.
Needs minutes of on-site exploration plus online fine-tuning per environment. The topological graph grows with experience and depends on the accuracy of learned distances.
